Kaneki Auth architecture

Architecture · proposal

Kaneki Auth: a free OIDC provider on Vercel, Neon and Better Auth

How the service is built, how external apps sign users in through it, how each app gets its own user pool, and what keeps it inside the free tiers.

  • Updated2026-11-10
  • StatusDraft, nothing built yet
  • Repokaneki-auth @ e059b9e
  • Budget$0 now · ~$10/yr later for a mail domain
  • Better Auth1.7.19

The design in one page

Short answer

Kaneki Auth is one Next.js codebase. It is deployed once per client app to Vercel's free Hobby plan, and each deployment has its own free Neon database, so every app has its own users. Each deployment runs Better Auth with the OAuth 2.1 Provider plugin, so it acts as a standard OpenID Connect server for its app. Users sign in with email + password, Google, or a magic link. S1S17S2

  1. One deployment per app is how each app gets its own users. Better Auth makes user.email unique across the whole database, and the organization plugin only groups one global user into teams. Separate users per app therefore means a separate database per app. S23S21 VERIFIED
  2. Tokens are JWTs only when the client asks for a resource. Without one, the access token is opaque and every API call needs an introspection request. Clients must always send resource. S18 VERIFIED
  3. Machine-to-machine: for service-to-API traffic, use client credentials. The JWTs are checked offline and the auth server is not called each time. Use API keys for scripts, admin calls and anything that needs per-key quotas. S18S20
  4. Yes, it needs interactive transactions. Sign-up, first social sign-in and password reset each write several rows as one unit. The Drizzle adapter has transactions off by default. Turn them on and use Neon's WebSocket Pool. S24S26S14 VERIFIED
  5. Email starts on Gmail SMTP and moves to Resend later. Resend needs a verified domain, and buying one is deferred. Until then mail goes through a personal Gmail account with an app password, which allows 500 emails a day. Mail sits behind a single sendMail() interface, so moving to Resend later is a config change. S32S33S35
  6. Neon compute is the tightest free limit. But the budget is per project, so each app's deployment gets its own 100 CU-hours. S13 VERIFIED
$0hosting + database per app
25apps max from one Git repo (Hobby)
100 CU-hNeon compute per app per month
500 / dayemails via Gmail SMTP (phase 1)

The big picture

Each deployment does three jobs: it shows the sign-in and consent pages, runs the OAuth/OIDC endpoints, and publishes the signing keys. The diagram shows one app's deployment. Every other app gets an identical copy (see one user pool per app).

The parts and why each was chosen

Each part is the free option that fits a stateless, serverless auth server. The brief fixes the three main choices. The rest are chosen to fit them. S1

How an external app signs a user in

An external app never sees a password. It sends the user to its Kaneki Auth deployment, gets back a one-time code, and swaps the code for tokens. Its API then checks those tokens locally.

Hover or tap a stage: AuthorizeSign in & consentCode exchangeCall & verify
  1. Authorize① ②

    The client creates a random verifier and hashes it into a code_challenge. It then redirects the browser to the auth deployment with its client_id, scopes and the resource (its API's URL). PKCE is required and only S256 is accepted. S2S18

  2. Sign in & consent③ ④ ⑤

    If the browser has no session yet, the auth deployment shows its sign-in page (password, Google, or magic link), then the consent page. Consent is stored per user and client, so the user is asked only once. S2

  3. Code exchange⑥ ⑦ ⑧

    The browser returns to the app with a one-time code. The app sends the code and the original verifier to POST /oauth2/token. It gets back an access token (1 h by default), an ID token, and, with offline_access, a rotating refresh token that lasts 30 days. S18

  4. Call & verify⑨ ⑩ ⑪

    The app calls its API with the access token. Because a resource was requested, the token is a JWT. The API fetches the JWKS once, caches it, and checks every later token's EdDSA signature without a network call. S3S18

    Examplejose.jwtVerify(token, createRemoteJWKSet(new URL("https://<app>-auth.vercel.app/api/auth/jwks")))
Watch outAlways send resource. Without it, the access token is opaque. The API then has to call /oauth2/introspect on every request, authenticating as a registered client, and each of those calls hits Vercel and Neon. S18S19

Registering a new external app

An admin registers each client through the plugin's admin client API. The admin sets its redirect URIs, scopes and client type. Leave open self-service registration (RFC 7591) off. Each app's origin also goes on trustedOrigins, because requests from other origins are blocked. S2S9

Sign-in methods and the mail plan

Two of the three chosen methods send email, and so does password reset. Email is therefore part of the core design. It starts on Gmail SMTP and moves to Resend once a domain is bought.

MethodPlugin / configEmails sentNotes
Email + passwordemailAndPasswordVerification (optional), password resetSign-up writes several rows in one transaction (see transactions). S24
GooglesocialProviders.google with clientId and clientSecretNoneCallback URL is https://<app>-auth.vercel.app/api/auth/callback/google. Set baseURL or the redirect will fail. S31 Google sign-in with an email that already exists is linked to that user automatically. S22
Magic linkmagicLink({ sendMagicLink })One per sign-inLinks expire after 300 s. A user is created on first use unless disableSignUp is set. Default limit is 5 requests per 60 s. S30
Why not Resend nowResend sends to anyone other than your own account address only from a domain you have verified with DNS records. A *.vercel.app name is assigned by Vercel and its DNS records are not yours to manage, so it cannot be that domain. S28S29 INFERRED (the Vercel docs never say outright that vercel.app records cannot be added. They describe DNS management only for domains you own)

The mail plan: one interface, two adapters

Better Auth never talks to a mail provider directly. It only calls the send callbacks you give it, such as sendMagicLink. S30 The names of the verification and reset callbacks are from memory and were not checked in the docs. INFERRED If all three callbacks call one sendMail() function, the provider becomes a detail of that one file.

Hover or tap a phase: Phase 1 · Gmail SMTPPhase 2 · Resend
  1. Phase 1: Gmail SMTP ($0)now

    Turn on 2-Step Verification on a dedicated Gmail account (not your personal one), then create an app password. App passwords "can only be used with accounts that have 2-Step Verification turned on". S34 Connect with nodemailer to smtp.gmail.com on port 465 (SSL) or 587 (STARTTLS). S36 Vercel blocks port 25, but "ports 465 and 587 stay open". S35

    EnvMAIL_PROVIDER=smtp · SMTP_HOST=smtp.gmail.com · SMTP_PORT=465 · SMTP_USER=…@gmail.com · SMTP_PASS=<app password>
  2. Phase 2: own domain + Resend (~$10.46/yr)later

    Buy the domain, add it in Resend, copy the DNS records Resend gives you, and verify. Then set MAIL_PROVIDER=resend on every app's deployment. Sign-in stays on vercel.app. The domain is used only for sending. S28

Machine-to-machine: client credentials or API keys?

Both work, and they solve different problems. Client credentials gives short-lived JWTs that APIs check offline, so it suits frequent service-to-API calls. API keys are long-lived secrets checked by the auth server on every use, so they suit scripts, admin calls and anything that needs per-key quotas.

Side by side

CriterionClient credentials (OAuth provider)API key plugin
Standard✓ OAuth 2.1 grant. Any OAuth library can use it. S18Better Auth specific. Sent in the x-api-key header. S20
Credential lifetime✓ Access token lasts 1 h (m2mAccessTokenExpiresIn), so a leak is short-lived. S18Long-lived, with an optional expiry. S7
Check cost per request✓ None when resource is sent, because the API verifies the JWT against the cached JWKS. S18✗ Each check is a call to /api-key/verify, which reads the database and updates usage counters. S20
Who it acts asThe client app itself, with no user. "A client_credentials JWT has no session." S18The user (or organization) that owns the key. S7
PermissionsAdmin-allowed client_credentials_scopes. openid, profile, email and offline_access are not allowed. S18Per-key metadata and permissions. S7
Quotas & rate limits✗ Not built in✓ Rate limits per key, plus a remaining count that can refill. S20
RevocationTakes effect when the token expires (≤ 1 h) INFERRED✓ Immediate, because every use is checked INFERRED
Setup per callerRegister a client and allow the grant. "A client cannot use the client_credentials grant until you allow it". S18Create a key and copy it once.

Use client credentials for…

  • An app's backend, cron job or worker calling that app's resource API
  • Any high-volume call. On the free tier, a check that skips the auth server costs nothing.
  • Callers that already have an OAuth library

Use API keys for…

  • Your own scripts and CLI calling the auth deployment's admin API
  • Low-volume integrations where pasting one secret is easier than an OAuth flow
  • Cases that need per-key quotas, refills or instant revocation
In shortDefault to client credentials with a resource. Use an API key only where an OAuth client is overkill or a quota is the point. Never put API keys on a hot path: each check costs a Vercel call and Neon compute.

One user pool per app

Separate accounts per app ("user A in app 1 and app 2 are two accounts") needs one Better Auth database per app. Multi-tenancy inside a single database is not the answer here.

Why the organization plugin does not fit

The organization plugin groups one global user into many organizations. Members are invited, and "a user is a member of" several organizations. S21 On top of that, the core schema makes user.email unique: true for the whole database. Two accounts with the same email cannot exist side by side in one instance. S23

Options for per-app user pools

OptionSeparate accounts per appUses Better Auth as designedFree-tier fitOps effort
A. One deployment + one Neon project per app✓ Separate databases✓✓ Each app gets its own 100 CU-h and 1 GB. Up to 25 apps per Git repo. S11S13N deployments and N migrations
B. One deployment, one Postgres schema per app, auth instance chosen by path✓✗ Custom multi-instance routing, not documentedAll apps share one compute budgetOne deploy, but custom code
C. Organization plugin✗ One global user S21✓✓Low
D. tenant_id column on user✗ email is unique for the whole table S23✗ Fights the schema✓High
RecommendationChoose option A. It uses Better Auth exactly as documented and isolates apps completely. It also multiplies the free Neon budget, since compute and storage are counted per project. The costs are one Vercel project, one Neon project and one set of env vars per app, plus running migrations against every database. A small script handles that. Reconsider option B only if you outgrow 25 apps per repo. S11S13

What is stored in Neon

Each app's database holds the same tables. Four core tables record who the user is and how they signed in, and the plugins add their own. The Better Auth CLI generates all of them, and Drizzle applies them. S5S6

Watch outMigrations: with Drizzle, run npx auth@latest generate, then npx drizzle-kit generate, then npx drizzle-kit migrate. The CLI's migrate command works only with the built-in Kysely adapter. Run migrations over Neon's direct connection, and repeat them for every app's database. S5S6S15

Does it need interactive transactions? Yes

Several Better Auth flows write more than one row and must succeed or fail as a unit. They run JavaScript between the queries, so they need an interactive transaction. Neon's HTTP driver cannot provide one.

Flows that Better Auth 1.7.19 wraps in runWithTransaction

FlowWrites inside the transactionSource
Email + password sign-upCreate user → link credential account → create sessionapi/routes/sign-up.mjs:144 S24
First Google sign-inCreate user → create accountoauth2/link-account.mjs:308 S24
Password resetConsume reset token → revoke sessions → write new passwordutils/password.mjs:32 S24
Update userUpdate user → refresh sessionapi/routes/update-user.mjs:173 S24
// src/lib/db.ts
import { Pool } from "@neondatabase/serverless";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/neon-serverless";
export const db = drizzle({ client: new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL }) });

// src/lib/auth.ts
database: drizzleAdapter(db, { provider: "pg", transaction: true }),

Simple single-row operations need no transaction even on Postgres. The Drizzle adapter's consumeOne and incrementOne are single atomic statements (DELETE … RETURNING and UPDATE … RETURNING), and it only opens its own transactions for MySQL. S26 PgBouncer's transaction pooling mode is built to carry transactions, so the pooled URL still works. S15

Trade-offHTTP is Neon's fastest mode for single queries. The WebSocket Pool costs a connection handshake on a cold function. That is the price of correct sign-ups, and it applies to every query because the adapter uses one driver. S14 INFERRED (latency not measured)

Rules that make it work on serverless

Vercel may run each request on a different short-lived instance. Every rule below follows from that.

  1. Connect through the pooler. Use the -pooler host. PgBouncer accepts up to 10,000 client connections, against 112 direct connections at 0.25 CU. S15
  2. Use the WebSocket Pool and transaction: true. See transactions. S14S26
  3. Store rate-limit counters in the database. The default in-memory store "may not be suitable … particularly in serverless environments". Set rateLimit.storage: "database". S8
  4. Keep sessions in Postgres, with no secondary store. If a Redis-style store is added later, also set session.storeSessionInDatabase: true, because the OAuth provider and API-key plugins need it. S2
  5. Run on the Node runtime, not Edge. In the Vercel Edge runtime, a WebSocket connection cannot outlive a single request. S14
  6. Run clean-up jobs daily at most. Hobby cron jobs run only once a day and may fire up to 59 minutes late. S12
  7. Expect a cold first request. Neon suspends compute after 5 idle minutes, and on Free this cannot be turned off. S13

Staying at $0: the free-tier budget

Each free plan caps a different resource. Neon compute runs out first, but it is counted per project, so each app has its own budget.

Free limits that matter (read on 2026-11-10)

ServiceLimitScopeRisk
Neon100 CU-hours / month S13per app (project)High
Neon5 GB transfer / month; 1 GB storage; 10 branches S13per app (project)Low
Neon100 projects; 20 GB storage in total S13accountLow
Vercel1,000,000 function calls; 4 CPU-hours active CPU; 100 GB transfer S10account (shared by all apps)Medium
Vercel25 projects per Git repo; logs kept 1 hour S11accountMedium
Gmail SMTP (phase 1)500 emails / day S33one Gmail account shared by all appsLow
Resend (phase 2)100 emails / day, 3,000 / month S16account (shared by all apps)Medium
In shortTraffic spread evenly through the day costs more Neon compute than the same traffic in bursts. JWT access tokens (always send resource), JWKS caching, and client credentials instead of API keys on hot paths are the main ways to save. INFERRED

When a limit is reached, Neon suspends that project's compute until the month resets. S13 A Vercel feature can stay blocked for up to 30 days. S10 Either way, sign-in fails for the affected apps.

Repository layout and environments

One Next.js codebase, deployed once per app. Only the route path comes from the Better Auth docs. The rest is a proposal. S4

kaneki-auth/
├─ src/
│  ├─ app/
│  │  ├─ api/auth/[...all]/route.ts   # export const { GET, POST } = toNextJsHandler(auth)
│  │  ├─ sign-in/page.tsx             # password, Google, magic link
│  │  ├─ consent/page.tsx             # "App X wants access to…"
│  │  └─ admin/…                      # client registration (admin only)
│  ├─ lib/
│  │  ├─ auth.ts                      # betterAuth({ plugins: [jwt(), oauthProvider(), magicLink(), apiKey(), admin()] })
│  │  ├─ db.ts                        # Neon Pool + drizzle (neon-serverless)
│  │  └─ email.ts                     # sendMail(): MAIL_PROVIDER=smtp | resend
│  └─ db/schema.ts                    # generated by `npx auth@latest generate`
├─ drizzle/                           # SQL migrations (drizzle-kit)
├─ scripts/migrate-all.ts             # runs migrations against every app's direct URL
└─ docs/architecture.html             # this file

Glossary

TermMeaning here
OIDCOpenID Connect: OAuth 2 plus an ID token that says who the user is.
PKCEA one-time secret the client creates for each login, which proves that the app swapping the code is the one that started the login.
resourceThe URL of the API a token is meant for. Sending it makes the access token a JWT.
JWKSThe published public keys that APIs use to check token signatures.
Client credentialsAn OAuth grant in which an app gets a token for itself, with no user involved.
Interactive transactionA transaction that keeps one connection open while application code runs between its queries.
User poolThe set of accounts one app sees. Here, one Neon project per app.
CU / CU-hourNeon compute unit. One CU-hour is one CU awake for one hour.
